prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows the camera wearer's extended right forearm and hand in the lower-middle foreground (roughly 0.2–0.5 m away, brighter at the lower wrist and fading toward the hand), holding a paintbrush against an indoor wall where it meets an overhead ceiling above and a window frame to the lower right. No other people are present, and the wearer's rest of body is out of view below the frame; the paintbrush and upper wall crease sit within arm's reach at roughly 0.4–0.6 m in front of the viewpoint. Across the five frames, the forearm and brush move slightly upward and rotate from a vertical stroke in frame 1 to an angled horizontal cut-in along the ceiling line in frames 2–4, then turn slightly left in frame 5 as the camera pans left to reveal a doorway edge on the far left. The depth map captures the smooth distance gradient along the reaching forearm and the recessed depth of the window on the right (frames 1–4) and doorway opening on the left (frame 5), which are low-contrast in the RGB image. However, the map is unreliable on the featureless white ceiling and upper wall—rendering the top ceiling as brightly as the near wrist while making the wall-ceiling corner artificially dark—and it blurs the thin paintbrush bristles into the wall surface in frames 1, 3, and 5.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates the camera wearer's reaching right arm in the lower-center foreground (extending from 0.2 m at the bottom edge to 0.5 m at the hand, facing away from the camera toward the wall) and the held brush at roughly 0.5 m, while leaving the wall, ceiling, and window in the background unsegmented. No other people are in the scene; the brush is held directly in the wearer's right hand with the handle extending to the lower right in frames 2–4 and partially occluded by the hand's grip in frames 1 and 5. Across the five frames, the segmented arm and brush reach upward toward the ceiling crease from frame 1 to frame 2, shift slightly right and angle horizontally through frames 3 and 4, and rotate back into a vertical grip in frame 5. The masks clearly delineate the boundary between the wearer's skin and the brush handle in frames 3 and 4 despite similar lighting and white paint tones against the wall in RGB. However, the segmentation is unreliable in classifying the paintbrush as a 'toothbrush' in frames 3 and 4, completely misses the brush in frames 1 and 5 (merging it into the 'person' mask in frame 1), leaves a gap over the brush handle in frame 2, and outputs duplicate overlapping 'person' labels in frame 3.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders only a magenta 3D hand skeleton for the camera wearer's right hand in the lower-central foreground at roughly 0.4–0.5 m distance, with no yellow body skeleton visible because the wearer's torso and head are outside the camera's field of view and no other people are present. The hand is positioned within arm's reach directly in front of the viewpoint and below the ceiling line, oriented with the back of the hand facing roughly toward the camera and the fingers curled around the paintbrush handle toward the wall. Across the five frames, the hand skeleton rises slightly from frame 1 to frame 2, tilts leftward in frames 2–4 to angle the brush bristles into the upper wall corner, and rotates more vertically and shifts upward in frame 5 as the wearer turns slightly left. Compared to the RGB strip, the skeleton explicitly reveals the 3D positions of the wrist, palm, and curled thumb and index joints even when fingers self-occlude or press behind the brush handle. It is unreliable in providing zero spatial information about the forearm, the held paintbrush, or the surrounding wall and ceiling geometry, and the finger keypoints compress into a tight, overlapping cluster in frames 2–4 where the pinch grip is viewed edge-on.
